Keywords: Forest Charter Venison Fines and Pledges
RagShortTexts: English forest law regulates resources, game and recognised local rights.
The Forest Charter limits abuses; not every forest offence brings death or mutilation.

Variants.Content: An English royal forest is a district under special law, not simply woodland: it can include grazing, villages and cultivated land. Forest law protects royal game and its habitat, but does not make all land and resources the king's property or erase established rights of grazing and collecting wood. The Charter of the Forest, issued in 1217 and reissued in 1225, restrains royal and official powers. Clause ten forbids loss of life or limb for the king's venison. A person with means pays a heavy fine; one without means is imprisoned for a year and a day, then released on finding pledges or required to leave the realm. By 1259, automatic blinding or mutilation for taking deer therefore misstates the rule. Clause nine protects free men's agistment in their own woods and passage of pigs; clause twelve permits works such as mills and ponds on their own land without harming neighbours. Rights depend on status, land and established use, not a general licence to kill deer or fell trees.

Holding land in a royal forest requires distinguishing ownership, royal game and recognised rights of use. The Forest Charter protects particular grazing and management rights and forbids loss of life or limb for venison, but retains fines, imprisonment and pledges. Defending a dependent requires evidence of land and custom, not merely claiming that the wood is one's own. Free men's protections cannot indiscriminately be applied to every tenant. An officer's demands and injury to neighbouring land are separate disputes requiring their own evidence.

A household living from a royal forest must distinguish recognised rights to wood, grazing and other resources from restrictions on game. By 1259 the Forest Charter already restrains certain abuses; not every infringement means immediate death or mutilation. An officer's demands remain frightening, and neighbours can quarrel over the same pasture. Poaching stories may celebrate courage, but bringing home meat does not legalise other uses. A family needs to know how the local court hears a claim and whether witnesses will testify before judging how much protection an ancient liberty really provides.
